lines.text: If a newly considered element has few measured properties, its group still gives useful predictions. What can the known members tell us?

Elements in the same group have the same number of outer shell electrons and often similar reactions. Follow an established trend down that group to predict a characteristic property, then explain the direction. For example, down Group two increased shielding and distance weaken attraction for outer electrons, ionisation energy generally falls and reaction with water generally becomes faster. Hydroxides generally become more soluble and carbonates more thermally stable. These are predictions from chemical periodicity, avoid claiming an unmeasured property was directly observed.
Across Period three you already used changing nuclear attraction to explain physical and oxide or chloride properties. Here the same periodic reasoning is extended to another member of a group.

Members of one group share an outer electron count. Use an established trend to predict a characteristic property. State the direction and explain it using structure and attraction. A prediction is an inference, so check its stated evidence.
Why would an element below barium in Group two be expected to react more readily with water?

Which evidence gives the most defensible prediction for the first ionisation energy of a Group one member below potassium, and why? The measured decrease from lithium to potassium, because increasing shielding and outer electron distance support extending the trend. The atomic radius of potassium alone, because one measurement fixes an exact ionisation energy for every group member. The shared outer electron count, because all Group one atoms must have identical ionisation energies. The increase in proton number alone, because shielding and electron distance can be ignored. ay A measured trend supported by atomic structure permits a cautious directional prediction. One radius gives no exact energy, a common outer electron count does not imply equal energies, and proton number alone omits shielding and distance.
An unknown element may fit one clue shared by several candidates. Combining clues can reveal its nature and position.

Deduce an unknown element by using all given physical and chemical properties. First infer a possible period from occupied shells or an across period trend, and a possible group from outer electrons or characteristic reactions. Then check each candidate against every observation before naming its identity. For example, both magnesium and aluminium ions can give a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Only aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess alkali, so that extra observation discriminates between them. A proposed identity must also fit any oxide, chloride, radius or ionisation energy clue. If the clues do not uniquely identify an element, give a possible position and explain the uncertainty.
This combines the Period three physical trends and the reactions of its oxides and chlorides into a single evidence based deduction.

Sort clues into period, group, physical and chemical evidence. Narrow candidates using shell count and outer electrons. Test every candidate against every observation. State nature, possible position and identity with supporting evidence.
Why is dissolution of a white hydroxide precipitate in excess alkali more useful than its colour alone?

Sodium and magnesium both form basic oxides that react with dilute acid. Which additional observation would distinguish the metals? Both samples conduct electricity as solids. Both atoms have three occupied electron shells. The large successive ionisation energy jump occurs after the first electron for one metal and after the second for the other. Both oxides form a salt and water with hydrochloric acid. C Sodium has one outer electron and magnesium has two, so their large ionisation energy jumps occur at different stages. Metallic conductivity, Period three shell count and basic oxide reactions are shared clues.
Describe how the tendency of Group two metals to react with water changes down the group.
Down Group two, the metals generally react more readily with water.

Element Q readily oxidises in air. The oxide produced reacts with water to form a solution of very low p H. Where could element Q be found in the Periodic Table? period group.
B is wrong because carbon dioxide forms a weakly acidic solution, not the very low p H described.

An element, Y, reacts according to the following sequence. Y white solid solution solution white precipitate burns in O two. H C L aqueous. N ay O H aqueous an excess of. N ay O H aqueous. What could be element Y?
B is wrong, magnesium hydroxide is a white precipitate but does not dissolve in excess sodium hydroxide.
Element X requires strong heating to react with oxygen. Element X reacts with chlorine to give a covalently bonded chloride. What could be the identity of element X?
Magnesium forms an ionic chloride, so ay is wrong, silicon forms a covalent chloride and needs strong heating with oxygen.

Compound X contains two Period three elements, Y and Z. Compound X reacts with water to form only two products, a slightly soluble hydroxide and compound Q. Q is a compound of element Z and hydrogen. Compound Q burns in moist air to produce an oxide and water. The oxidation number of element Z in the oxide is plus five. Which row identifies element Y and element Z? element Y element Z.
Magnesium phosphide gives slightly soluble magnesium hydroxide and phosphine, sodium compounds do not give that hydroxide.
The trends seen in Group two can be used to predict the properties of radium and its compounds. Which statement is correct?
Radium is predicted to react faster with water. B is wrong because Group two hydroxides become more soluble down the group.

Scientists are trying to synthesise a new element with proton number one hundred and nineteen. The element is predicted to be a Group one element in Period eight of the Periodic Table. Which predictions are likely to be correct about this element? one. The outermost occupied orbital of one atom of this element will be an s orbital. two. The atomic radius will be the largest of the seven elements in Group one. three. It will have a greater first ionisation energy than element one hundred and eighteen.

Element X has the second largest atomic radius in its period. An atom of X has three occupied electron shells only. The oxide of X is shaken with water. What could be the p H of the resulting solution? fourteen.

X, Y and Z are elements all found within Groups thirteen, fourteen and fifteen of the Periodic Table. X is in the same group in the Periodic Table as Y. Y and Z are in Period three. The first ionisation energy of X is greater than the first ionisation energy of Y. The melting point of Z is less than the melting point of Y. Y and Z both form chlorides which are white solids. These white solids react with water to produce solutions with a p H of less than four. Which row of the table shows the possible identities of X and Y? Y. X. aluminium. B.

An unknown metal X has three occupied electron shells. Its first three successive ionisation energies are approximately seven hundred and forty, one thousand four hundred and fifty and seven thousand seven hundred and thirty kilojoules per mole. Its oxide reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to form a salt and water. part a, Deduce its period and group, explaining each inference. part b, Identify X and write the equation for its oxide with hydrochloric acid. part c, Explain why sodium fits the oxide observation but cannot fit all the clues.
Shell count fixes the period, the large successive ionisation energy jump fixes the outer electron count. Magnesium satisfies both, whereas acid reaction alone also fits sodium.
Use the shell clue and the energy clue separately before combining them.
Compare the size of each successive energy increase, then check how a basic oxide reacts with acid.
The largest jump marks the start of removing inner shell electrons, count how many electrons were removed before it.

An unknown solid metal Y is one of lithium, sodium or magnesium. Each atom has one outer shell electron. Its oxide reacts with water to form an alkaline hydroxide solution. part a, Deduce its group and reject one candidate with a reason. part b, A student says the oxide observation proves Y is sodium. Justify whether this conclusion follows. part c, State one further piece of atomic information that would distinguish the remaining candidates, with the result for each.
The electron clue eliminates magnesium, but the chemical clue is shared by both remaining candidates. Shell count or proton number would resolve the ambiguity.
Ask which clue rules out a candidate and which clue might be shared.
Check each remaining candidate against both observations, rather than choosing the first that fits.
A shared reaction cannot separate candidates, look for an atomic property that changes between periods.

Rubidium lies immediately below potassium in Group one. Potassium has outer electron arrangement four s to the power of one. part a, Predict the outer electron arrangement of rubidium and compare its atomic radius with potassium. part b, Predict its relative reactivity with water under comparable conditions and explain using shielding, distance and electron loss.

Moving from potassium to rubidium adds an occupied shell while retaining one outer s electron. Greater distance and shielding make loss of that electron easier, supporting the predicted increase in reactivity.
Locate rubidium relative to potassium and consider what changes on entering a new period.
Compare the principal shell of the outer electron and the shielding provided by inner shells.
The relevant process in reaction with water is loss of the outer electron, compare the nuclear attraction holding it.

A table gives measured first ionisation energies for lithium, sodium and potassium as five hundred and twenty, four hundred and ninety six and four hundred and nineteen kilojoules per mole, respectively. No value is supplied for rubidium, immediately below potassium in Group one. part a, State the observed trend and make a cautious prediction for rubidium relative to potassium. part b, Explain the prediction using atomic structure. part c, Explain why neither an exact value nor a claim that rubidium has been measured follows from these data.

The measured sequence supports a downward extrapolation, explained by shielding and outer electron distance. Unequal changes and the absence of a rubidium measurement limit the conclusion to a qualitative prediction.
Separate the entries actually measured from the element whose value is missing.
Compare successive entries and ask whether their differences are constant.
Only the direction of the supplied sequence is established, extending it requires an assumption about continuation.
nine point three Chemical periodicity of other elements.
In one breath.

An element's position in the Periodic Table gives a basis for predicting its characteristic properties. To identify an unknown, combine several physical and chemical clues, then check that the proposed element fits every one.
Key ideas.

Elements in one group have the same number of outer shell electrons, which explains many similarities in chemical properties. A measured trend among known group members can be extended cautiously to predict a member for which data are not supplied. A prediction should state both the direction of a property change and the reason for it.

Down Group two, increasing distance and shielding make outer electrons easier to remove. First and second ionisation energies generally decrease, and reaction with water generally becomes more vigorous. Group two hydroxides generally become more soluble down the group, while carbonates become more thermally stable. Thus an element below barium is predicted to react faster with water and form a more soluble hydroxide and more thermally stable carbonate than barium. These are predictions from trends, not direct observations of every possible element.

Across Period three, atomic radius generally decreases from sodium to chlorine because nuclear charge rises while electrons are added to the same principal shell. Sodium has the largest atomic radius and magnesium the second largest. Three occupied electron shells place an atom in Period three. The number of outer electrons then helps establish its group.

Chemical behaviour supplies further clues. Magnesium and aluminium ions can each give a white hydroxide precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Aluminium hydroxide dissolves in excess aqueous sodium hydroxide, magnesium hydroxide does not. Silicon forms covalent silicon tetrachloride and needs strong heating to react with oxygen. The Period three chlorides and oxides therefore help narrow an unknown's identity, but one clue alone may be shared by several elements.
Method.
Extract each observation separately. Mark whether it indicates a period, group, physical trend, or chemical reaction.
Use electron shells or an atomic radius ranking to narrow the period. Use outer electrons and known group behaviour to narrow the group.
Test each candidate against every observation. Eliminate a candidate as soon as one definite clue contradicts it.
State the possible position and identity, then justify them with the most discriminating evidence. If evidence allows more than one element, say so.
Worked example.

An unknown Period three metal forms a white oxide. Its aqueous ions give a white precipitate with aqueous sodium hydroxide, which dissolves in excess alkali. Deduce the metal. A white precipitate alone is not decisive because both magnesium and aluminium ions can form one. Dissolution in excess alkali identifies amphoteric aluminium hydroxide. The metal is aluminium, its white oxide agrees with the other clue.
Traps.
Trap, Treat a white hydroxide precipitate as proof of aluminium. Why it's wrong, Magnesium hydroxide is also white. Instead, Check whether the precipitate dissolves in excess alkali.

Trap, Reverse a group trend for an unfamiliar element. Why it's wrong, A prediction should follow the established trend unless evidence says otherwise. Instead, Write the direction down the group before comparing candidates.
Trap, Identify an element from one clue and ignore the rest. Why it's wrong, Individual properties are often shared. Instead, Check all physical and chemical observations.
Exam technique.

For predict, give the likely property and the trend used. For deduce, show how the clues restrict period, group and identity. For explain, link a trend to nuclear attraction, distance or shielding, as appropriate. Distinguish an observation from an inference, a white precipitate is observed, while aluminium is a deduction that needs the excess alkali result.
